title: Touching and wudu
hookLine: schools differ on whether touching certain things breaks wudu

cards: A couple heads out the door for the evening prayer. Both have just made wudu, the washing before prayer: hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, feet. At the door, one reaches for the other's hand.

Then a pause. Does that touch mean washing again before praying? Ask a Shafi'i teacher, a Hanafi teacher and a Maliki teacher, and you may get three different answers, each with a verse and a report behind it.
It sounds like the smallest question in the world. It's a doorway into how the schools read one word.

teach.b: In surah five, the Qur'an lists the things after which a believer who can't find water should use clean earth instead, and one of them is a phrase built on the verb lamasa: when you have touched women.

teach.h: A POLITE WORD, OR A HAND?
teach.b: A report from Ibn Abbas takes it as a polite way of naming intercourse, the way English says two people slept together. Others among the Companions, tradition says, took it as touch by hand.
Hanafi scholars follow the first reading: a touch of the hand doesn't break wudu.

They also point to Aisha's report in Sahih al-Bukhari: she lay in front of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ while he prayed at night, and when he went down to prostrate, he touched her feet so she would draw them in, and he kept praying.
Shafi'i scholars take touched as touch: skin on skin with an unrelated adult of the opposite sex breaks wudu, desire or not.
Maliki and Hanbali scholars stand between: the touch breaks wudu when it comes with desire. Ja'fari jurists hold that touching doesn't break it at all.

teach.h: BUSRA AND TALQ, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: Last, a second case, with two reports side by side. Busra bint Safwan reports that whoever touches his private part should make wudu. Talq ibn Ali reports the Prophet asking, isn't it just a part of you?
Shafi'is and Hanbalis lean on Busra; Hanafis on Talq. The details differ. The washing stays.

how: Each school teaches its own list of what breaks wudu: in the Shafi'i school skin contact with an unrelated adult of the opposite sex does, in the Maliki and Hanbali schools only touch with desire, and in the Hanafi and Ja'fari schools touch alone does not.

o: the washing of hands that must come before eating any meal
a ban on shaking hands with anyone in the mosque
whether a touch breaks wudu, a question the schools answer differently

games.q: touching and wudu — tap the pairs.
p: breaks when it comes with desire

s: every school agrees that any touch breaks wudu
Shafi'is say skin contact does; Malikis and Hanbalis only with desire; Hanafis and Ja'faris say touch alone doesn't.
Aisha reports the Prophet touched her feet while praying at night and kept praying
Hanafi scholars point to this report in Sahih al-Bukhari.
the two reports from Busra and Talq say the same thing
Busra's report calls for wudu after touching the private part; Talq's asks, isn't it just a part of you?

games.q: you're a jurist reading the verse 'when you have touched women.' Ibn Abbas says it means intercourse. others say it means touch by hand. what do the schools do?
o: each weighs the readings and reports, and they land in different places.
vote and make one rule for all.
games.why: Hanafis follow Ibn Abbas, Shafi'is take it as touch, Malikis and Hanbalis add desire, and Ja'fari jurists say touch doesn't break wudu.

practice: If you follow a school, ask yourself honestly whether you know what it teaches about touch and wudu.
If you don't, recall one small rule you grew up with, shoes off at the door, no hat at the table, the first bite for the eldest, and ask whether you know the reason behind it.
Hold the rule and its reason for a few breaths, without judging either.

wordCard.voice: Touching and wudu. Whether a touch breaks the washing before prayer: by one reading, it doesn't; by another, skin on skin does; by another, only with desire. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: touch; the verb lamasa stands behind the verse the schools read differently.

carryVoice: Your line: details differ. Every small rule has a reading behind it. Same time tomorrow.
